title: Charter Check-in
note: Scenario questions on the charter check-in, written for study: taking over a bareboat at the base — papers, the walk-round, engine, electrics, water and gas, instruments, safety gear, ground tackle — and handing it back. Not an IYT course and not any charter company's procedure; the contract and the base's briefing are the authority. figure is a spec for docs/design/figures.js (null = text question). Pass mark, exam size and time are app defaults.

questions.q: The base's confirmation e-mail reminds you to bring your papers to check-in. What goes in your hand luggage?
options: Your skipper's licence, VHF certificate, every passport and the crew list
The boat's registration and insurance, printed from the base's website
Your logbook and the sailing-school certificates of each crew member
Your own passport only — the base has the crew from the booking form
questions.why: The base checks the skipper's licence and VHF certificate and files a crew list with passport numbers for the port police.

questions.q: You fill in the crew list at the desk and the manager asks whether anyone else will sleep aboard this week. What do you say?

figure.title: Crew list
lines: A friend joins Wednesday in Lefkas
Two crew fly home on Thursday
Port police may check at any harbour

options: Yes, but you will write him on the list yourself when he arrives
Yes — name the Wednesday guest now and tell the base again when the crew changes
No — a guest for two nights is not crew and does not go on the list
No — the list is for the people who signed the charter contract
questions.why: Everyone who sleeps aboard is on the crew list; a change mid-week is reported to the base, which amends the list for the port police.

questions.q: Reading the deposit clause, your crew ask what it costs if the dinghy flips and the outboard goes to the bottom. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Contract — deposit
lines: Held on card or in cash at check-in
Limit of liability for insured damage
Dinghy and outboard: at full value

options: Half the price — the base shares losses that are nobody's fault
Nothing — the boat's insurance covers the tender and its motor
The full price of the outboard — the deposit does not cap a lost dinghy or outboard
At most the deposit — that is exactly what the deposit is for
questions.why: The deposit caps insured damage only; the contract lists what is charged in full — negligence, grounding, the dinghy and outboard.

questions.q: The desk offers you this waiver. Your crew say that with it nothing can be charged to you. What do you tell them?
options: They are right — the waiver replaces the deposit and ends your liability
It covers the hull only; everything else comes off the full deposit
It is the boat's insurance; without it the base cannot let you sail
It lowers the deposit, but the items listed as excluded are still charged in full
questions.why: A waiver cuts your exposure, not the exclusions: negligence, grounding, dinghy, outboard and sails stay on the charterer.

questions.q: The technician hands you this folder at the chart table. Where does it live during the week?
options: In the chart table, aboard, ready for a port police check in any harbour
At the base — the originals are too valuable to take to sea
In your bag, to show at the desk when you hand the boat back
At the marina office of your first harbour, with the crew list
questions.why: The boat's papers sail with the boat: port police check the registration, insurance, radio licence and charter permit.

questions.q: Your crew want to cross to Italy on Tuesday night and be back by Thursday. You read this clause. What do you do?

figure.title: Contract — navigation limits
lines: No sailing between sunset and sunrise

options: Go by day only — the clause forbids night sailing, not the crossing
Ask the base for written consent before you leave; without it the crossing is off
Go — the limits bind the boat's insurer, not the skipper
Go, and call the base from Italy so that they know where the boat is
questions.why: Outside the contract area or at night the insurance and the deposit cap fall away; only the base's written consent moves a limit.

questions.q: Your crew point at the late-return clause and say you must leave now. What do you do?

figure.title: Thursday 07:00, Kioni
lines: Forecast: NW 6–7 all day and Friday
Contract: no leaving port above F6

options: Leave under engine only — the wind limit is about sailing, not motoring
Leave at once with two reefs — the wind limit is advice, the penalty is money
Stay in port, call the base now and agree with them what happens about the return
Leave on Friday at dawn instead; one day of F7 is a smaller risk than two
questions.why: A wind limit in the contract is a limit; the base would rather move the return than have the boat out in F7.

questions.q: The manager runs through the chart briefing fast, pointing at the wall chart. What do you do with what he says?

figure.title: Chart briefing
lines: Reef off the cape: keep 0.5 M off
Bay with the cable: no anchoring

options: Note the no-go areas only; the rest is local colour
Photograph the wall chart and work out the details at sea
Listen — the pilot book covers it all and you can read it on passage
Write it on your chart as he goes and ask him to repeat anything you missed
questions.why: The chart briefing is local knowledge the pilot book lacks: hazards, no-go bays, harbours untenable in a given wind.

questions.q: The technician offers to do the technical briefing on the pontoon in five minutes, 'since you have sailed this type before'. What do you say?

figure.title: Technical briefing
lines: Gas: bottle in locker, valve under sink

options: Ask to go through each system aboard, hands on, with every switch and valve shown
Accept, but ask for the briefing on paper to read on passage
Accept, and read the owner's manual aboard tonight instead
Accept — the same model has the same systems at every base
questions.why: Every charter boat is wired and plumbed differently; switches, valves and quirks are shown aboard by the one who knows them.

questions.q: The manager ends the briefing with this slide. What do you do with it every morning of the week?
options: Look at the sky and the barometer; forecasts are for open-sea crossings
Check the named sources before deciding the day's passage, and call the base if in doubt
Wait for the base to call before leaving harbour each day
Check your phone's weather app — the sources listed are for the base's own use
questions.why: The briefing names the forecasts the base trusts for its area; the daily decision to sail starts with them.

questions.q: On Wednesday the forecast shows a gale for Friday, so you plan to be back at the base on Thursday evening. What does the contract say about that?

figure.title: Charter contract — return
lines: Return: Friday by 18:00, at the base
Early return: no refund of unused days
Late return: a fee per hour started

options: The unused day is refunded at the daily rate
You must stay out until the return time in the contract
Nothing is refunded for the unused day; the berth is yours from Thursday — tell the base you are coming
The deposit is reduced by one day's charter
questions.why: Coming back early is your call and costs nothing extra; unused days are not refunded; call the base so a berth is free.

questions.q: Your crew want to spend Friday night in a bay an hour from the base — the flights are not until Saturday noon. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Contract — times
lines: Boat in base marina: Friday by 18:00
Late return: a penalty per hour, plus costs

options: Fine — the base can check the boat out in the bay if you call them
Fine, if you leave the bay at 06:00 and refuel on the way in
Fine — check-out is at 09:00 and an hour's sail gets you there in time
No — the boat is in the base marina on Friday evening; Saturday morning is the check-out
questions.why: The contract wants the boat back the evening before: the base checks her out, refuels and cleans her before the next crew.

questions.q: The technician fills in the form as you walk round and hands it to you to sign. What do you do before you sign?
options: Read every line against what you saw, add what is missing, then photograph the form and the boat
Sign — the technician's copy is the one that counts and he has written it all down
Sign, and e-mail the base a list of everything else you can remember
Sign, and photograph the boat later in the evening when it is quieter
questions.why: The check-in form is what the deposit is settled against; anything not on it counts as new damage at check-out.

questions.q: Your partner also holds a licence and will skipper half the week. The contract looks like this. What do you do?

figure.title: Charter contract — crew
lines: Crew: 6 adults on the crew list

options: Nothing — once the skipper is checked, anyone aboard may take the helm
Have the base add them as co-skipper now, licence shown, before the contract is signed
Carry their licence aboard and show it only if the port police ask
Add their name to the crew list and leave the contract as it is
questions.why: Only the skipper named in the contract is covered at the helm; a co-skipper is added at the base, with their licence, before signing.

questions.q: At the office the desk asks you to sign the contract and the check-in form together, 'the technician will walk you round afterwards'. What do you do?
options: Sign neither until the technician has walked you round the boat
Sign both — the walk-round is a formality and the form can be amended by e-mail
Sign the contract; the check-in form only after the walk-round, with what you found on it
Sign both, and photograph the boat so that you have your own record
questions.why: The check-in form records the state of the boat as you took her over; it is signed after the walk-round, not before.

questions.q: It is 19:30 on Saturday, the base is handing over twelve boats, and the technician says 'she's fine, sign here, I'll come by tomorrow if anything is wrong'. What do you do?
options: Sign — he has seen the boat, and you will phone the base about anything tomorrow
Refuse to sign, sleep ashore and come back on Sunday morning when it is quieter
Sign now, then e-mail the base a list of defects first thing on Sunday
Walk round yourself now, write what you find on the form, and have the base countersign it tonight
questions.why: The walk-round is yours, not the base's; what is not written and countersigned before you sign is yours to pay for.

questions.q: Friday 16:00, the base is in sight and the tank is at three-quarters. Where do you take the boat first?

figure.note: Fri 18:00, tanks full · base refuels at fuel + €80

options: A — fill up, then berth at B and report to the base
B — berth; the base's refuelling costs the same as the pontoon
C — the visitor quay for the night; the return berth is for Saturday
B — berth; the base fills up from the berth on Saturday morning
questions.why: Full to full: the boat comes back with full tanks; refuelling by the base is charged on top of the fuel.

questions.q: Your crew say you can hand-haul the anchor all week and mention the windlass on Friday. What do you do?

figure.title: Tuesday, Vathi, 12 M from base
lines: Windlass stops with 20 m of chain out
Contract: no sailing with a known fault

options: Hand-haul for the week and write the windlass on the check-out form
Call the base now, report it, and sail on only as they instruct
Sail on to the next big harbour and find a mechanic there yourselves
Open the windlass and repair it yourselves so that nothing is charged
questions.why: Under the contract the skipper reports a fault at once and does not carry on with it; the base decides the repair.

questions.q: The other skipper is holding out the cash. What do you do?

figure.title: Wednesday, Fiskardo
lines: A departing motorboat hits your bow
Their skipper offers €200 cash to settle
Base number on the chart table

options: Take the cash and write the damage on the check-out form on Friday
Let him go, and have the pulpit straightened at the yard here today
Refuse the cash, take the boat's name, port, insurer and photos, and call the base at once
Take the cash — it will cover the gelcoat and the base need not know
questions.why: A third-party collision is settled between insurers: the base needs the other boat's details, photos and your report at once.

questions.q: In your first harbour the port police come aboard and ask for the boat's papers. What do you hand them?

figure.title: Port papers
lines: Transit log, stamped at the base

options: A photo of the papers on your phone; the originals stay at the base
The charter contract — it shows that the base is responsible for the boat
Your skipper's licence and passport — the rest is the base's business
The document folder: transit log, crew list, registration and insurance
questions.why: Port police check the transit log and crew list against the registration and insurance; they must be aboard and current.

questions.q: It is 16:30 at the base in Lefkas. The technician hands you the form and says he will start with the engine. How do you run the walk-round?

figure.title: Check-in, Lefkas
lines: Form: boat outline and a remarks box
Three more boats waiting for him

options: Outside first from the quay, bow to stern on both sides, then the deck, then the rig
Engine and inside first, the hull from the quay once he has left
Whatever order he prefers, as long as the engine runs before you sign
Deck and rig first while it is light, the hull from the dinghy tomorrow
questions.why: A fixed order — hull both sides, deck, rig — is how nothing gets missed; the hull is the deposit.

questions.q: At 17:10 the technician says this and heads for the next boat. What do you do?

figure.title: Technician
lines: 'Walk round yourself, I have three more'
'Bring the form to the office by 18:00'
Form still blank for hull and deck

options: Agree; a photographed walk-round is as good as a witnessed one
Ask him to stay for the walk-round — what you find alone is disputed on Friday
Walk round alone and list everything; the office will accept the list
Sign the hull section now and photograph the boat after he leaves
questions.why: Damage goes on the form with the base's technician present and initialling; notes made alone are your word against theirs.

questions.q: On the port bow, 40 cm aft of the stem, you find this. It is not on the form. What do you do?

figure.title: Port bow: gelcoat chip 3 cm
lines: Below the toe rail, 40 cm aft of the stem
Form: nothing marked at the bow

options: Write 'scratches, port bow' in the remarks box and move on to the deck
Ask the base to fill and polish it before you leave the dock
Photograph it with a coin for scale, write 'chip 3 cm, star cracks' on the outline, have him initial
Leave it — chips under 5 cm are normal wear and are never charged
questions.why: Size, place and a photo with scale; star cracks mean impact, so write cracks, not scratches.

questions.q: From the quay you look along the port side at the waterline. What goes on the form?

figure.title: Waterline, from the quay
lines: Stern 5 cm low: tanks full, 6 bags aboard
Stbd quarter: brighter gelcoat patch, sound

options: Nothing — the waterline and old repairs are not deposit items
'Crack, starboard quarter' — so the repair cannot be charged to you later
A request for a diver before you sign — fouling slows the boat and heats the engine
'Weed on waterline' and 'old repair, stbd quarter' with a photo — neither is yours
questions.why: Fouling and old repairs are the base's; writing them down with a photo is what keeps them the base's.

questions.q: Moored stern-to in Alimos, the water is clear enough to see the keel. What do you do before you go aboard?

figure.title: Stern, from the quay
lines: Keel leading edge: scuffed, paint gone

options: Photograph both, write them on the form, and watch the rudder while he turns the wheel lock to lock
Note the rudder only; the keel is below the waterline and is not on the form
Ask for a haul-out before you accept the boat — a scuffed keel means a grounding
Note nothing; the technician has seen the keel and says it is only sand
questions.why: A keel scuff at check-in that is not on the form becomes your grounding at check-out.

questions.q: You check the bathing platform before the crew arrives with the bags. What do you ask for?

figure.title: Bathing platform
lines: Platform hinge: 1 cm play, lifts with a clunk

options: Nothing fixed — write all three on the form and manage with a bucket
The rung and the shower head fixed before you leave; the hinge play on the form with a photo
A tape repair on the rung yourself; note the hinge and the shower
The hinge rebuilt before you leave; the rung and the shower are wear
questions.why: A cracked rung breaks under a wet crew member; the rest is noted so it is not charged on Friday.

questions.q: You lean on the starboard guardrail by the gate and find this. What do you do?
options: Write all three on the form and seize the hook with a lanyard
Tell the crew to use the port side and note it on the form
Ask the base to fix all three before you leave — the guardrail is what keeps the crew aboard
Tighten the stanchion yourself; the wire and the hook are cosmetic
questions.why: A loose stanchion or a frayed lifeline fails when someone falls on it; the base fixes it, not the form.

questions.q: In the forecabin you look at the hatch and the portlight. What do you do?

figure.title: Forecabin hatch
lines: Lens: 8 cm crack from the hinge corner
Seal perished; hatch does not dog down tight

options: Ask for the portlight handle freed; the hatch is noted as wear
Note the crack; keep the hatch shut all week and the bunk stays dry
Note all three and ask for a tarpaulin for the foredeck
Photograph the crack and ask for the lens taped and the seal replaced — a wave fills that bunk
questions.why: A hatch that does not seal takes green water on the foredeck; a cracked lens is a deposit item unless noted.

questions.q: Walking the port side deck you press with your heel by the chainplates. What goes on the form?

figure.title: Side deck, port
lines: Non-slip worn smooth by the shrouds
Soft spot 20 × 20 cm by the chainplate
Genoa track: two bolts standing proud

options: All three with photos; the soft spot and the raised bolts the technician initials
Nothing — deck wear is never a deposit item
The soft spot only — worn non-slip and proud bolts are wear
A request for the deck re-cored before you sail
questions.why: A soft spot is structural and may be blamed on your week; written and initialled now it stays the base's.

questions.q: You open the cockpit lockers against the inventory. What do you do?

figure.title: Cockpit lockers
lines: Lazarette: padlock missing, lid does not latch

options: Note 'lockers OK'; a lid that does not latch is tied with a line
Count against the list; ask for a padlock, a latch that holds and the drain cleared
Ask for everything moved to the saloon so you can count it
Sign the inventory — the count is the base's job, the latch you tie down
questions.why: An unlatched locker lid opens at sea and floods the lazarette; a blocked drain floods the cockpit.

questions.q: At the binnacle you turn the wheel and work the lever with the engine off. What do you ask for?

figure.title: Binnacle
lines: Wheel: a quarter turn of play before the rudder moves
Wheel lock: slips under hand pressure
Throttle: stiff, two hands into astern

options: The wheel lock replaced before you leave; play is normal, the lever you learn
Nothing adjusted — note all three, charter wheels are always loose
The steering cables and the throttle cable adjusted now; the lock on the form
A spray of lubricant on the lever yourself; note the play and the lock
questions.why: Play in the steering is a loose cable or chain; a stiff throttle costs the moment you need astern in a berth.

questions.q: You check the canvas before the afternoon sun goes. What do you ask for?

figure.title: Sprayhood & bimini
lines: Sprayhood window scratched; port zip open at the foot
Bimini frame bent; one strap missing
Bimini: 15 cm tear at the aft seam

options: Nothing fixed — canvas is wear, write all five items on the form
A new bimini fitted before you leave the dock, the sprayhood noted
The tear only; the zip, strap and frame are how the boat came
The zip, strap and tear fixed before you leave; the window and the frame on the form with photos
questions.why: A tear grows in the first blow and a missing strap lets the bimini fold; what cannot be fixed now goes on the form.

questions.q: You check the standing rigging at deck level on both sides. What do you do?

figure.title: Standing rigging, from deck
lines: Port cap shroud: turnbuckle split pin missing, no tape
Starboard lower: one broken strand at the swage

options: A broken strand means the base's rigger before you sail; the split pin and tape are fitted now
Ask for the rig tuned and tensioned before you accept the boat
Note both; tape the strand and ask for a split pin at your first port
Fit a pin yourself; one broken wire of nineteen is fine for a week
questions.why: A broken strand at the swage is the start of a failure; a turnbuckle without a split pin unwinds.

questions.q: You stand at the mast foot on deck. What do you check by eye?
options: The wind vane turning; the rest needs a bosun's chair
Up the groove: a straight mast, spreaders level with boots on; the collar sealed, the deck flat round the foot
Count the halyards and read the makers' label at the gooseneck
Push the mast at the gooseneck to feel for play in the step
questions.why: A bend, a drooping spreader or a dished deck round the foot are seen from the deck; the base's rigger does the rest.

questions.q: You swing the boom and look at what holds it up. What do you ask the base for?

figure.title: Boom
lines: Gooseneck pin: worn, boom knocks when swung
Rigid kicker holds the boom; no topping lift
Preventer: no line aboard, no pad-eye forward

options: A new gooseneck fitting; the preventer is for ocean passages, not the Ionian
Nothing — all three are how the boat was built and how it sailed last week
The gooseneck pin looked at now and a long line to rig a preventer; the rigid kicker needs no topping lift
A topping lift rigged to the masthead; the gooseneck play is normal and a sheet makes the preventer
questions.why: A rigid kicker carries the boom; a worn gooseneck pin and no preventer are what hurt crew in a gybe.

questions.q: At the cabin-top winches you run each halyard and clutch. What do you do before you sign?

figure.note: Clutch #2 jammed shut · 2 of 3 winch handles found

options: Sign — a jammed clutch is opened at sea with a winch, two handles are plenty
Ask for the halyard replaced and a new self-tailer; the handle you buy
Note all four on the form and free the clutch with pliers once out
The clutch freed and the third handle found now; the chafe and the jaws on the form
questions.why: A clutch that will not release is a halyard you cannot drop; a missing handle is a deposit charge on Friday.

questions.q: At the bow you work the roller, the stopper and the cleat by hand. What do you do?

figure.title: Bow fitting
lines: Bow roller: pin bent, roller does not turn
Port bow cleat: moves under hand pressure

options: Ask for all three fixed before you leave — the cleat and the stopper take the mooring and anchor loads
Note all three; the windlass holds the chain and the starboard cleat does for mooring
Ask for the roller only; a loose cleat and a stopper are the base's wear
Tighten the cleat from below yourself and note the roller and the stopper
questions.why: The chain stopper, not the windlass, holds the anchor load; a loose cleat is a line gone in a Meltemi night.

questions.q: The technician says the masthead was checked at the start of the season. How do you check it yourself before you sign?
options: Send a crew member up in the bosun's chair with the technician on the winch
Through binoculars from the quay: wind vane and cups turning, VHF antenna upright, light lenses whole
Switch the instruments on — a wind reading means the masthead is fine
You cannot from the deck; write 'masthead not inspected' on the form
questions.why: Binoculars show a missing cup, a leaning antenna or a cracked lens from the quay; the season's start was months ago.

questions.q: You find the pulpit bent to port. The technician says this. What do you do?

figure.title: Pulpit bent to port
lines: Technician: 'That's old, it's on the form already'
Form, boat outline: nothing at the bow

options: Take his word — he knows the boat and the office has last week's form
Write it in the remarks box as 'general wear' to match the office
Write 'pulpit bent, port' on the outline now, photograph it and have him initial
Ask the office for last week's check-out form before you continue
questions.why: What counts on Friday is this form; 'general wear' and the technician's memory are not entries.

questions.q: In the catamaran saloon you find this, and the manager wants the form signed before the briefing. What do you do?

figure.title: Saloon forward window
lines: Crack 25 cm from the lower corner
Manager: 'sign now, we correct it Monday'

options: Sign with 'see photo' beside the entry; the photo is dated and the office has a copy
Sign; a correction on Monday is in writing and better than an argument now
Sign and e-mail the office the photo tonight so the record is complete
Do not sign until the entry reads 'crack 25 cm' with your photo — 'scratched' is your crack on Friday
questions.why: You sign for the boat as the form describes it; a crack recorded as a scratch is charged to the deposit.

questions.q: Saturday, 16:30, light wind. The technician ticks 'Sails: OK' and says they were checked yesterday. What do you ask for before you sign?

figure.title: Check-in form — sails
lines: Wind at the pontoon: F2, no swell
Main in the stackpack, genoa furled

options: The main hoisted and the genoa unrolled now, while it is calm
Nothing — it was checked yesterday and the form says OK
To unroll them yourself on the first morning and phone in faults
A look inside the stackpack and the sail bags, unhoisted
questions.why: Sails are checked hoisted: at the pontoon in light wind, not at sea; a faulty sail found on Sunday is your problem.

questions.q: The genoa is fully unrolled. You look at the furling drum and see this. What do you ask for?

figure.note: Genoa fully out · rest of the line slack on deck

options: The slack on deck coiled, tied off to the pulpit and left
The line rewound tight on the drum with the sail fully out
Three turns taken off the drum so the sail unrolls fully
Nothing — the drum should be empty when the sail is out
questions.why: With the sail fully out the drum must hold enough line to roll it all in; one turn left means the line runs out mid-furl.

questions.q: Halfway through furling the genoa the line goes solid. The technician reaches for a winch handle. You look up and see this. What do you do?

figure.title: Genoa furler — jammed
lines: Halyard wound twice round the forestay above the swivel
Furling line: solid, two turns on the drum

options: Note 'stiff furler' on the form and grease the swivel yourself once at sea
Let him winch it — a halyard wrap pulls itself out once under load
Stop him — unroll, clear the wrap, and have the base fix the halyard lead
Sheet the genoa in hard on the winch to drag the wrap down the foil
questions.why: A halyard wrap jams the swivel; winching it damages the foil and the halyard. The halyard angle at the masthead is the base's job.

questions.q: The technician runs the genoa sheet through the car for you. You check the car itself and see this. What do you ask for?

figure.note: Starboard car lashed to the track with cord · port car OK

options: The port car moved across to starboard; one car is enough
A shackle through the car to the toe rail once at sea
Nothing — the cord lashing holds the car where it is
The plunger pin replaced so the car locks in the track
questions.why: A car that is not pinned slides under load: the sheet lead goes and the car can hit the end stop; the pin is a base fix.

questions.q: The genoa is out. You walk the leech and see this. What do you do?

figure.title: Genoa leech
lines: UV strip: stitching gone along 1.5 m, strip hanging
Leech line: cleat at the clew broken, line flapping

options: Photograph both, note them on the form, ask for the strip restitched today
Nothing — the UV strip is cosmetic and a leech line is only a trim aid
Tape the strip down and tie off the leech line yourself, then move on
Sign now and mention both at check-out if they have got any worse
questions.why: A loose UV strip tears off and takes stitching with it; the leech line flogs the leech. Both are quick fixes at the base, not at sea.

questions.q: At the genoa clew you find this. The technician says it has sailed like that all season. What do you do?

figure.title: Genoa clew
lines: One loop chafed through, one frayed
Sheets tied with bowlines, no shackle

options: Accept it — two of the three loops are still holding the ring
Insist the base repairs the clew now — it carries the whole sheet load
Tie the sheets to the ring with a round turn and two half hitches instead
Note it on the form and ask for a reduced deposit for the week
questions.why: A clew lets go in a gust and the sail flogs itself to pieces; a chafed clew is the base's repair, not a note.

questions.q: The main goes up at the pontoon and you see this. What do you ask for before you sign?

figure.title: Mainsail hoisted
lines: Batten 3: snapped, bends in the middle
One luff slide cracked; stackpack zip slider missing

options: The zip fixed now; battens only matter with the full main up
Everything on the form — you will be sailing on reef 1 most days anyway
Battens and the slide replaced now; the zip photographed and on the form
A spare batten and a spare slide to fit yourself at the first anchorage
questions.why: Missing battens let the leech flog and tear; a cracked slide jams the hoist. The zip only keeps the cover shut.

questions.q: You run the genoa sheets to the winches and look at them. What do you ask for?

figure.note: Port 14 m · starboard 16 m · spare lines: list 2, found 1

options: The port sheet end-for-ended so the chafe sits at the tail end
Both sheets swapped for the spare lines and the old sheets noted on the form
Nothing — a sheet lasts the week; the spare takes over if it goes
The port sheet replaced and the second spare line found before you sign
questions.why: A bare core fails under load and a 14 m sheet will not reach the winch on a wide genoa; spares are counted, not assumed.

questions.q: The boat has in-mast furling. The technician asks you to unfurl the main yourself. How do you do it?

figure.note: In-mast main · outhaul on the winch, furling line in a clutch

options: Outhaul out on the winch, the furling line eased with a little tension kept on
Furling line cast off fully first, then the outhaul hauled out on the winch
Outhaul winched out with the furling line still shut in its clutch
Furling line and outhaul hauled together so the roll stays tight
questions.why: The roll must stay firm as it leaves the mast: slack on the furling line lets it bunch and jam in the slot; never winch against a closed clutch.

questions.q: Now the technician furls the main back in. You watch the boom and the lines. What do you ask him to change?

figure.title: In-mast main — furling in
lines: Topping lift eased: boom end below horizontal
Furling line pulled fast, by hand

options: Furling line pulled faster, two hands, so the roll stays tight in the mast
Boom up to the base's mark on the topping lift, a little outhaul tension kept
Boom lower still on the topping lift so the sail drops into the mast on its own
Outhaul let fully go so that nothing at all resists the roll into the mast
questions.why: The boom at the set angle feeds the luff square into the slot; a loose roll creases and jams, and a jammed furler is never forced.

questions.q: The technician points at the clutches and says 'reefs are there'. What do you ask for before you sign?
options: The colour code written on the form so you can look it up when you need it
The reef lines coiled and stowed below; you will try them out at sea
Reef 1 put in at the pontoon, so you see which line does what and runs free
A spare clutch handed over in case one of the reef clutches fails at sea
questions.why: A reef is practised at the pontoon in calm, not worked out at 25 knots; a jammed reef line is then the base's fix.

questions.q: You look at the gooseneck and the reef lines. What does this tell you about reefing at sea?

figure.title: Reefing gear
lines: Cockpit: one line per reef, to the clew cringle

options: The luff reefs with the halyard alone; the horns are spare fittings, unused
Single-line: one pull from the cockpit reefs both the luff and the clew together
The horns take the tack only; the reefs are single-line, pulled from the cockpit
Two-line: the luff cringle is hooked on a horn at the mast, then the clew line hauled
questions.why: Horns at the gooseneck mean the luff is hooked by hand: plan who goes forward, clipped on, before you need a reef.

questions.q: The main is sheeted in at the pontoon and you see this. What do you settle with the base before you sign?

figure.title: Boom & bimini
lines: Main sheeted in: boom end 3 cm above the bimini frame
Bimini: folds aft in a minute

options: Whether the bimini folds under sail or the boom is held clear — and who pays if it tears
Nothing — it is only canvas; the boom slides over it on a gybe without harm
The boom held up high on the topping lift and cleated there for the whole week
The bimini taken off and left ashore at the base for the week, fitted again on Friday
questions.why: A boom that meets the bimini on a gybe tears it, and the damage comes off your deposit; agree the rule now, in writing on the form.

questions.q: The genoa is out in F2 and the luff looks like this. The technician says it always does. What do you do?

figure.title: Genoa luff
lines: Genoa halyard: in a clutch at the mast

options: Ease the backstay a turn — the scallops come from forestay sag, not from the halyard
Tension the halyard until the scallops just go, then check the furler still turns
Leave it — a slack luff rolls up tighter on the furler and sets better
Winch the halyard bar-tight; a furling genoa can never be too tight
questions.why: Scallops mean a slack luff; set the halyard so they disappear, no more — an over-tight halyard stiffens the furler and wraps.

questions.q: Your check of the mainsheet, traveller and vang gives this list. What goes to the base to fix now, and what on the form?

figure.title: Mainsheet, traveller, vang
lines: Mainsheet lower block: one cheek cracked
Traveller control line: cover chafed, core sound

options: Everything on the form — nothing has actually failed yet, so nothing to fix
The chafed line replaced now, the block noted — rope fails before metal
The cracked block replaced now; the chafed cover photographed and on the form
Both replaced now before you sign, or you do not take the boat at all
questions.why: A cracked block under mainsheet load can burst and hurt someone: repair now. A chafed cover on a sound core: note it, watch it.

questions.q: The inventory lists a preventer. You find this in the cockpit locker. What do you ask for?

figure.title: Inventory — deck
lines: Preventer line: 1 — found: 6 m, snap hook

options: A second 6 m line so you can rig one on each side at the same time
A boom brake instead of it; a preventer line is only for racing boats
Nothing — 6 m from the boom end to the toe rail amidships is how it is rigged
A line long enough from the boom end to the bow and back to a cockpit winch
questions.why: A preventer runs from the boom end forward to the bow and back aft, so it can be eased from the cockpit; a short strop to the rail breaks the boom.

questions.q: The inventory lists the sails below. You open the forepeak. What do you do before you sign?

figure.title: Inventory — sails
lines: Found: bag 'Gennaker' (sail + sock); bag 'Storm jib' — empty

options: Have the storm jib found or struck off the list, and the count on the form
Sign — you will not fly a storm jib in August in the Ionian anyway
Count the bags, not the contents: two bags on the list, two bags found
Take the technician's word that it is in the office and will be put back
questions.why: What is on the signed list is what you hand back on Friday; a sail you never had is charged against your deposit.

questions.q: Sunday, your first sail. Off the headland the genoa furling line goes solid with the sail half rolled. What do you do?

figure.title: Day 1 — off Lefkas
lines: Genoa half rolled, furling line solid

options: Cut the furling line at the drum and roll the sail by hand round the foil
Ease the sheet, try again by hand, and call the base for instructions — cut nothing
Leave it half out, hoist the main and carry on under both to the anchorage
Put the furling line on the electric winch and grind the sail in, turn by turn
questions.why: A jammed furler is a base problem: forcing or cutting it turns a phone call into a damaged foil and a deposit claim.

questions.q: On the 42 ft catamaran the technician says 'the main goes up like on any boat'. You look at the lazy bag and the head of the sail. What do you ask to see?

figure.title: Catamaran mainsail
lines: Square-top main: headboard on two cars
Lazy bag zip: 2.6 m above the coachroof
Boom reached from the coachroof steps

options: Only the sail number on the bag — a catamaran's main hoists like any other mainsail does
That the bag can stay zipped shut and the main hoisted straight up through it
The main hoisted and dropped once: how the square top goes into the bag, and where you zip it
A ladder added to the inventory so you can reach the zip from the deck at anchor
questions.why: A square top with two headboard cars needs the lazyjacks and the bag opened right, at a height; see it done once at the pontoon.

questions.q: At the briefing you are given this. What does it mean for your week?

figure.title: Contract & briefing — wind
lines: Sailing permitted up to F6 on the base forecast
Reef 1 at 18 kn, reef 2 at 25 kn
Above F6: stay in port, call the base

options: The reef numbers apply only with the full genoa out; with the main alone they do not
The limit is for the forecast only; at sea you carry on as you judge best
Reef when the boat feels overpressed; the numbers are a guide for beginners
Reef at those numbers and stay in port above F6 — they are contract terms, not advice
questions.why: Sailing above the contract limit, or unreefed when told to reef, can void the insurance and put the damage on you.

questions.q: The technician lifts the companionway steps and lets you pull the dipstick and open the header tank yourself. What do you ask for before you sign?

figure.title: Engine bay, before starting
lines: Dipstick: at the top mark, milky grey
Belt: firm, a little black dust

options: The base to find why the oil is milky and to fill the coolant before you leave
Nothing — oil goes grey after a season of short runs in the marina
To run the engine hot for ten minutes and look at the dipstick again
A litre of coolant to top up yourself, with the oil colour noted on the form
questions.why: Milky oil is water in the oil — a heat exchanger or gasket fault; the base fixes it, not you at sea.

questions.q: You look round the engine with a torch while the technician waits. What do you ask for?

figure.title: Engine bay — hoses and tray
lines: Coolant stain under one hose clip
Raw-water seacock: under the sole, open
Tray: a film of old oil

options: Nothing — a stain and a film of oil are normal on a charter engine
The clip tightened and the tray wiped dry, so a new leak will show this week
The seacock closed while in port and opened before each start
A rag over the tray so the oil does not reach the bilge pump
questions.why: Small leaks are noted and fixed at the base; a dry tray is how you spot a new one on day three.

questions.q: The technician has already filled in the engine hours on the check-in form. You look at the panel. What do you do?
options: Write both numbers on the form and let the base manager choose
Sign the form — the base counts hours from its own log
Have the form corrected to the panel reading and photograph the panel
Note the difference and raise it at check-out if hours are charged
questions.why: Engine hours on the form are what you are charged against at check-out; write what the panel shows, with a photo.

questions.q: The technician hands you the key: 'Start it yourself.' In what order do you do it?
options: Key on and crank straight away — a warm Greek engine needs no preheat
Lever a little ahead so it does not stall, key on, crank at once
Throttle wide open in neutral, crank until it fires, then back off
Lever in neutral, key on, wait for the glow-plug light to go out, then crank
questions.why: Neutral, preheat, crank: a diesel starts in neutral and the glow plugs need their seconds, even in summer.

questions.q: The engine has started under the technician's eye and you watch the panel. What do you do?
options: Pull the stop handle now — the alarm should stop within seconds as oil pressure rises
Turn the key off and on again to reset the alarm and carry on
Let it idle five minutes; the buzzer stops once the oil is warm
Rev it to 1,500 so the pressure builds faster and the buzzer stops
questions.why: The oil alarm sounds until pressure builds — a second or two; longer than that, stop the engine before it damages itself.

questions.q: The engine is running at the pontoon. You step aft and look at the exhaust outlet: a puff of smoke, no water. The technician says 'give it a minute'. What do you do?
options: Rev it to 2,000 for a moment so the pump pulls the water through
Have the engine stopped now and the seacock, strainer and impeller checked before it restarts
Give it the minute — raw water takes time to come up through the strainer
Note 'no exhaust water' on the form and check again at the fuel quay
questions.why: No water at the exhaust means no cooling: a closed seacock, a blocked strainer or a dead impeller — stop first, find out second.

questions.q: The technician reads the spares list off the inventory. What do you ask for before departure?
options: A second belt — belts go more often than impellers in the heat
A bottle of coolant and a funnel for the header tank
A spare impeller and the tools to fit it, and where the puller is kept
Nothing — the base's mechanic comes out if anything fails
questions.why: The impeller is the usual cause of overheating; without a spare aboard a failure ends the day's sailing where you are.

questions.q: The contract says the boat is handed over with a full tank. What do you do?
options: Accept his word — gauges on charter boats are never trusted anyway
Sign for full and put in a claim at check-out if it runs short
Fill it yourself on the first day and keep the receipt for the base
Ask to see it dipped or topped up at the fuel quay, and write the gauge reading on the form
questions.why: 'Full on handover, full on return' only works if you see it full: a dip, a sight glass or a visit to the fuel quay.

questions.q: Your plan for the week is about 6 hours of motoring a day for six days. What do you decide at the briefing?
options: Plan a fuel stop around midweek — 36 hours is about 144 litres of a 160-litre tank
Refuel only when the gauge first shows a quarter, as on a car
Run the tank down and fill it once on the way back on the last day
Nothing — a 160-litre tank is more than a week of motoring on a 45-footer
questions.why: 36 h × 4 L/h = 144 L: the week's plan uses the whole tank minus reserve, and the gauge cannot be trusted to warn you.

questions.q: The technician shows you the deck fillers on the side deck. What do you do?
options: Remember 'fuel is port' — the technician knows his boats
Open the port one and smell it, mark it with tape and show the crew which is which
Let the fuel attendant find the right one; it is his job at the quay
Ask for both caps to be changed to marked ones before departure
questions.why: Diesel in the water tank ruins the week's water and the tank; mark the fuel filler and brief the crew before anyone fills anything.

questions.q: You look at the primary filter with a torch while the technician talks you through the fuel shut-off. What do you ask for before you sign?

figure.title: Fuel system
lines: Bowl: dark layer at the bottom
Fuel shut-off: on the tank, open

options: The shut-off closed overnight to keep water out of the lines
A spare element so you can change it yourself if the engine falters
The bowl drained and the element changed now, and the change written on the form
Nothing — a little sediment in the bowl is normal after a season
questions.why: The dark layer is water or sludge; it reaches the injectors in the first rough sea — the base deals with it at the pontoon.

questions.q: At the pontoon with the lines on, the technician clicks the lever ahead: the revs rise, the boat hardly pulls and something clunks under the stern. What do you ask him to do?
options: Rev harder in ahead until the clunking stops and the lines come tight
Pull the button on the lever hub — it is in throttle-only mode and needs the gear in
Sign for it — the gear works, the boat is just held by the lines
Go to neutral, give a burst astern to open the folding propeller, then try ahead again
questions.why: A folding prop's blades can stick half-open from the marina; astern opens them. Test ahead and astern with the lines on, before you leave.

questions.q: After ten minutes running at the pontoon the panel looks like this. The technician says 'the light always does that'. What do you do?
options: Ask for the belt and alternator checked before you leave — it is not charging
Idle the engine an hour at tick-over tonight and see if the light goes out
Accept it — a 12.1 reading with the engine running is a healthy battery
Switch to the house bank and let the charger pick it up on shore power
questions.why: A battery light with the engine running means no charge: a slipping belt or a dead alternator. With it, the week ends on day two.

questions.q: The technician runs the engine in gear against the lines while you look under the aft cabin bunk. What do you say?

figure.title: Shaft and gearbox
lines: Engine running: a steady trickle at the seal
Bilge: 2 cm of water, pump cycling
Gearbox oil: at the mark, clear

options: A few drips a minute are normal on a stern gland — write 'OK' on the form
A dripless seal should be dry — ask the base to look at it and amend the form before you sign
Ask for the bilge pump set to automatic and sail; the seal is doing its job
Tighten the seal's collar a quarter turn yourself until the trickle stops
questions.why: A packed gland drips a little; a dripless seal does not. A trickle plus a cycling pump is a fault for the base to fix at the pontoon.

questions.q: The boat is afloat; the technician ticks the underwater lines from memory and asks you to sign. What do you write?
options: 'Checked by base' so the responsibility stays with them
Nothing extra — you will check it on the first swim and amend then
'Not seen' against each underwater line, and sign only for what you were shown
'OK' — the base lifted the boat in the spring and knows the anode
questions.why: You sign for what you saw. An anode or a prop you did not see is 'not seen' on the form, or it is yours at check-out.

questions.q: The technician closes the port engine hatch and moves on to the electrics. What do you ask?

figure.title: 42 ft catamaran — engines
lines: Stops: pull handle at each panel

options: Whether the two hour counters can be reset to match for the form
Which engine to run alone on passage to keep the hours even
Nothing — twin engines are the same; one is a spare for the other
To see the starboard engine too — it has its own strainer, filter, stop and start battery
questions.why: Two engines means two of everything: each is checked, each hours reading goes on the form, and each stop is found before you leave.

questions.q: The technician points at the bow-thruster switch at the helm: 'Test it yourself.' How do you test it at the pontoon?
options: Switch it on, a short burst each way with the lines on, watch the bow wash, then switch it off
Take his word for it — a thruster is either fine or the base knows
Leave the test until you are clear of the pontoon with room to move
Run it a full minute each way so you know the battery can take it
questions.why: Short bursts: a thruster overheats in a minute of running. Its own breaker and battery are shown to you at the same time.

questions.q: You read the clause before signing. Your plan has two long motoring days. What do you do?

figure.title: Contract, clause 11 — engine
lines: Engine use: max 4 h per day

options: Sign as it is — most days you will sail, so the two long days are covered
Ask the base manager whether the 4 hours is per day or averaged over the week, and get the answer on the form
Ask for the clause to be struck out since a sailing yacht is not a motorboat
Sign and keep your own log of hours to argue from at check-out
questions.why: A clause means what the base says it means — in writing, before you sign, not at check-out when the excess is on the bill.

questions.q: The engine has been running a quarter of an hour at the pontoon. The technician says the sender has been like that all season. Do you accept the boat?
options: Yes, with a discount on the charter price written into the contract
Yes — the base knows its engine; note 'oil alarm, faulty sender' on the form
Not until the base proves the oil pressure, replaces the sender or gauge, and writes it on the form
Yes, if he pulls the buzzer fuse so the crew are not alarmed at sea
questions.why: An oil alarm you cannot tell from a real one is no alarm: you would not know at sea. Not a boat to sign for.

questions.q: Day three, motoring towards the harbour, the panel changes to this. What do you do?

lines: Buzzer sounding; steam at the exhaust

options: Slow to tick-over and carry on; the temperature will fall at low revs
Keep going at 2,200 — the engine will last the last two miles to the harbour
Sail the last miles and restart the engine only for the mooring
Throttle back, neutral, stop; let it cool, then check strainer, impeller and belt before restarting
questions.why: Overheat: stop before it seizes. Sail or anchor, find the cause (strainer, impeller, belt), call the base if it is beyond you.

questions.q: The technician opens the battery lockers of the catamaran and shows you this. What do you want to be sure of before he closes them?
options: That each engine has its own starter battery and the house bank is separate from both
That the port engine battery also runs the fridge, being the strongest one
That all five batteries are wired as one bank, for the most capacity
That the house bank starts the engines when the starter batteries are low
questions.why: Separate banks: a flat house bank after a night at anchor still leaves each engine its own battery to start.

questions.q: The technician shows you the battery switches and gives you this advice. How will you actually run them?

figure.title: Battery switches
lines: Technician: "just leave BOTH on all week"

options: ENGINE off at anchor so the fridge and the lights cannot flatten the starter battery
ENGINE and HOUSE on at sea and at anchor; BOTH only for a flat-battery start; all off leaving the boat
HOUSE off under way so the alternator puts the whole charge into the engine battery
BOTH on all week, as he says, so the fridge and the lights can draw on both banks together
questions.why: Both banks on keeps them separate; BOTH joins them, so a flat house bank takes the engine battery with it.

questions.q: First morning at anchor; you read the battery monitor before switching anything on. What state is the house bank in?
options: Flat — anything under 13 V needs the engine now
Overcharged — a bank at rest should read 12.0 V
Full — a rested bank at 12.7 V is near 100 %
Half — 12.7 V is midway between flat and full
questions.why: Rested, no load: 12.7 V full, 12.4 V about 75 %, 12.2 V half, 12.0 V or less flat.

questions.q: At check-in the technician points at the voltmeter and says the batteries are 'perfect'. What does this reading actually tell you?
options: That the bank is full and will hold 13.8 V all night at anchor
That the batteries are new — an old bank never gets up to 13.8 V
That the bank is being overcharged and the charger must go off now
Only that the charger is working — the state of the bank shows after a rest off the charger
questions.why: On charge the charger sets the volts (13.8 float, 14.4 bulk); the bank's own voltage is read after an hour at rest.

questions.q: You are going through the panel with the technician and see this. What do you do?
options: Note it on the form and ask the base to sort it before you sail — the charger is off or the bank is dead
Switch to BOTH so the engine battery carries the house bank for the week
Move the cable to another pedestal socket, see the light come on and sign
Accept it — the bank will come up once you run the engine on Sunday morning
questions.why: Plugged in, the bank should read 13.8–14.4 V; 11.8 V with current going out means no charge — and ask how old the bank is.

questions.q: The technician waves at the panel, says 'all the usual' and heads for the engine bay. What do you ask him to do first?
options: Leave every breaker on so you can find out as you go
Switch on each breaker in turn and show you what it feeds
Explain the 230 V side only — the 12 V side is obvious
Hand you the boat manual to read the panel on passage
questions.why: You will be finding these at night in a blow; VHF, instruments and the windlass each have their own breaker.

questions.q: Your crew asks whether the kettle and the hairdryer will work in the bays. What do you tell them?

figure.title: Main panel
lines: Right: 230 V AC — RCD, charger, outlets, water heater
Inverter 300 W: one socket at the chart table

options: Yes — flip the 230 V main breaker and the batteries feed the outlets directly
Yes — switch the charger on and it converts 12 V into 230 V for the outlets
Only on shore power — at anchor the 230 V outlets are dead and the inverter runs a laptop, not a kettle
Yes with the engine running — the alternator powers the 230 V side of the panel
questions.why: The 230 V side is live only on shore power or a generator; a 300 W inverter will not run a 2 kW kettle.

questions.q: The technician plugs the shore cable in and goes to fetch the inventory list. You look at the 230 V panel. What do you do?
options: Press the RCD test button to clear the warning and carry on
Turn the plug the other way round in the pedestal socket
Ignore it — polarity only matters on American 110 V boats
Unplug it and tell the base — the pedestal is miswired; no 230 V until it is fixed
questions.why: Reverse polarity leaves the live side on breakers that should be neutral; an RCD does not make it safe.

questions.q: Sunday 10:00, the technician has gone and you are ready to cast off from the pontoon. In what order do you deal with the shore power?
options: Charger and 230 V main off, pedestal switch off, unplug the pedestal end first, then the boat end, stow the cable
Pull both ends, leave the cable on the pontoon for the base to collect, cast off
Leave it plugged in until the engine is running for a last charge, then pull both ends at once
Unplug the boat end first, hand the live cable to a crew on the pontoon, then the pedestal end
questions.why: Dead before you touch it, pedestal end first so no live plug lies on deck; the cable is on the inventory.

questions.q: You ask the technician to start the engine and watch the battery monitor. What do you tell him?
options: All good — it charges the engine battery, which is not on this monitor
It is not charging — the alternator or belt needs looking at before you leave
All good — volts must drop a little when the engine takes its load
All good — the alternator only starts charging above 2000 rpm
questions.why: With the engine running the monitor should show about 14 V and current going in; 12.3 V and −8 A is no charge.

questions.q: The technician resets the breaker, the windlass runs, and he moves on. What rule do you take away, and what do you ask before he goes?

figure.title: Windlass
lines: Breaker 80 A at the chart table
Tripped on the first test, reset

options: Use it with the engine off at anchor so the alternator is unloaded; and the make of the motor
Start the engine only if it stalls; and whether the house bank can be switched in to help it
Engine running whenever you use it; and where the spare fuses are, for anything that blows instead of tripping
Breaker on all week so the remote always works; and whether the base will come out if it trips again
questions.why: The windlass draws 80–100 A; the alternator covers it and the engine is ready. A breaker resets, a fuse needs a spare.

questions.q: Evening in the bay, the fridge is the only thing running. Do you leave it on overnight?
options: No — switch it off at night; 5 A will flatten 200 Ah well before dawn
Only with BOTH selected so the engine battery shares the night's load
Yes, and the lights and the inverter too — 200 Ah is enough for the week
Yes — about 5 A for 10 h is 50 Ah, a quarter of the bank; charge with the engine in the morning
questions.why: Amps × hours = amp-hours; a lead-acid bank should not go below half, so 50 Ah of 200 is fine.

questions.q: Saturday night you switch on NAV LIGHTS and walk out along the pontoon to look at the bow. This is what you see. What do you do?

figure.note: Pontoon, 21:00 — seen from ahead, NAV LIGHTS on

options: Note the dead starboard light on the form and ask the base to replace the bulb before you sail
Accept it — you plan to be in a harbour every night
Sail with the tricolour instead — it shows the same arcs
Buy a bulb in town on Monday and fit it yourself
questions.why: Test the lights at the pontoon, at night, from outside; the base replaces what is dead.

questions.q: You switch on the ANCHOR breaker and look up from the pontoon. What have you confirmed?
options: The tricolour works — show it at anchor to save the battery
The all-round white anchor light works — the one to show every night at anchor
The steaming light works — the one to show at anchor with the engine off
The deck light works — enough for a quiet bay with no traffic
questions.why: At anchor at night a vessel shows an all-round white light (Rule 30); test it where you can see it.

questions.q: The technician reads this off the inventory list without opening the floor. How do you check it before you sign?

figure.title: Bilge pump
lines: Electric: float switch in the bilge
Hand pump in the cockpit, handle in the locker

options: Trust the panel light — it only comes on if the pump is wired
Leave it on AUTO and look at the bilge again at check-out
Switch to ON and hear it run, lift the float for AUTO, find the hand-pump handle
Set it to OFF so it cannot drain the batteries at anchor
questions.why: A pump that was never heard is a pump that may not run; AUTO stays selected all week.

questions.q: What do you do with these two before you sign, and what do you ask?

figure.title: Alarms
lines: Gas detector: sensor in the bilge, panel at the galley
CO alarm in the saloon, 9 V battery

options: Note that they are fitted — testing them trips the panel breaker
Ask for a spare detector in case this one goes off falsely
Take the battery out of the CO alarm so it does not chirp at night
Press TEST on each and hear it; ask what to do when the gas alarm sounds
questions.why: Gas alarm: close the bottle valve, no switches, ventilate; a dead CO alarm goes on the form.

questions.q: The technician says 'you will not need these' and skips them. What do you ask him to show you anyway?

figure.title: Also fitted
lines: Solar 200 W on the bimini, controller at the chart table
Generator strainer under the aft bunk

options: The solar controller charging, and the generator started with water at its exhaust; note the hours
The generator fuel level only; a solar panel has nothing to check
Nothing — extras you do not use are not your problem at check-out
The panel wiring under the bimini, with the controller switched off
questions.why: Anything on the inventory is yours for the week; a generator is checked like the engine — hours and raw water.

questions.q: The technician brings this cable to plug you in. What do you do?

figure.title: Shore cable
lines: Outer sheath cut, copper showing near the plug

options: Use it with dry hands and keep the cut end on the boat, not the pontoon
Refuse it and ask for another — a damaged 230 V cable on a wet pontoon can kill
Plug it in only at night when nobody is walking along the pontoon
Tape over the cut and plug in — the RCD will trip if anything leaks
questions.why: 230 V, seawater and bare copper: no tape, no dry hands; the base has another cable.

questions.q: The technician lifts the bunk and shows you the batteries. What do you do?

figure.title: Battery compartment
lines: Under the aft bunk, terminals uncovered
Master switches: behind the companionway steps
Technician: "check they are tight if you like"

options: Ask him to disconnect the bank so you can inspect each battery
Check the terminals are tight with the winch handle while he watches
Ask him to show you the master switches and fit terminal covers; you do not touch the terminals
Note it and plan to buy terminal covers in town on Monday
questions.why: A dropped spanner across the terminals is a fire; in a fire you must find the master switch in the dark.

questions.q: The technician asks how you plan to run the boat for the week. What is your plan?

figure.title: Power budget
lines: Fridge 5 A · instruments 2 A · lights 2 A · autopilot 4 A

options: Fridge off, autopilot on all night — the autopilot matters more
Run everything — 200 Ah will see the week out without charging
Keep the engine idling all night so the fridge never drains the bank
Engine an hour morning and evening, fridge on, instruments and autopilot off when not needed
questions.why: About 100 Ah usable; a day's draw is near that, so charge twice a day and cut what is not in use.

questions.q: The technician says both water tanks are full. The panel shows this. What do you do before you sign?
options: Switch the selector to tank 2 and look into both fillers yourself
Ask him to top up tank 1 and sign
Note 'gauge faulty' on the form and sign
Sign — the gauge reads the tank not in use
questions.why: A gauge reads the selected tank; a quarter-full tank 1 is the first thing to see — check both tanks at the filler before signing.

questions.q: On the side deck you find three deck caps; the lettering has worn off. Your crew is already uncoiling the pontoon hose. What do you do?
options: Fill the aft one; water fillers are always aft
Have the technician identify each cap and mark it before any hose goes in
Try each cap — water goes in the one that gurgles
Fill the biggest cap; the water tank is the largest
questions.why: Water in the diesel tank or the holding tank ends the week; caps are marked WATER, DIESEL, WASTE — if they are not, mark them.

questions.q: You are filling the water tanks at the pontoon with the marina hose. How do you do it?
options: Fill only the tank the selector is on; the other fills by itself
Fill through the galley tap so the pump stays primed
Run the hose clear first, then fill each tank until it overflows at the filler
Put the hose in, go to the shop and come back in an hour
questions.why: A hose that has lain in the sun holds stale water; fill to overflow, tank by tank, and stay with it.

questions.q: Every tap is closed, yet the pressure pump keeps running. The technician says it is just priming. What do you do?
options: Leave it; a pump stops by itself once it finds pressure
Sign and switch it off at night to save the batteries
Open a tap to let the air out and let it run on
Switch the pump off and ask the base to find the leak before you leave
questions.why: A pump that runs with the taps closed is pumping into a leak or from an empty tank — on a full tank, that water is going into the bilge.

questions.q: Monday morning at anchor. Your crew report this. What do you do?
options: Run the engine for half an hour — the heater element only works on shore power
Switch on the inverter so the heater element can run
Report it to the base as a broken water heater
Open the hot tap and wait; the element takes an hour
questions.why: The calorifier is heated by the engine's cooling water or by a 230 V element on shore power; at anchor only the engine heats it.

questions.q: You are leaving the pontoon. The heads bowl is full of water and the pump lever is on 'wet'. What do you do?
options: Pump the bowl full so the seal stays wet at sea
Pump the bowl dry and set the lever to 'dry'
Set the lever to 'dry' and leave the bowl full
Leave it; the water keeps the smell down
questions.why: A full bowl slops and can siphon when the boat heels; at sea the bowl is pumped dry and the lever left on dry.

questions.q: A crew member reads the sign over the heads and asks whether the wipes she bought can go in. What do you answer?
options: Yes, in the electric heads but not in the manual one
Yes, if the packet says 'flushable' and you pump well
No — only what has been eaten and a little paper; wipes go in the bin
Yes, one at a time with plenty of pumping after it
questions.why: Wipes do not break up; they block the pump and the holding tank, and the contract charges you for the unblocking.

questions.q: Sunday afternoon in a bay. The crew are going ashore for lunch and the boat will be empty for three hours. This is how you leave it. What do you change?

figure.title: Leaving the boat, 13:00
lines: Gas valve at the bottle: open

options: Close the seacocks; the pump must stay on for the fridge
Close the gas valve; the rest is fine for three hours
Switch the pump off; seacocks stay open to vent the heads
Close the heads seacocks and the gas valve, and switch the pump off
questions.why: An empty boat is left with seacocks shut, gas off at the bottle and the pressure pump off: nothing can flood or leak while nobody is aboard.

questions.q: The technician shows you the holding-tank valve in this position, in the marina. What do you do?
options: Set it to 'tank' now and open it only when you are well offshore
Leave it; direct overboard saves pumping the tank out
Leave it in the marina; switch to 'tank' once at sea
Set it to 'tank' and never open it; the base pumps out
questions.why: In harbour and in bays everything goes to the tank; the valve is opened only offshore, where the briefing allows discharge.

questions.q: At check-in the holding tank reads this. The technician suggests you empty it at sea tomorrow. What do you do?
options: Sign and open the valve at the first bay tomorrow
Ask the base to pump it out before you sign; a full tank is not an accepted boat
Sign and note 'tank full' so the return check is fair
Sign, and empty it over the side tonight after dark
questions.why: You take over a boat with an empty holding tank; discharging in a bay or a harbour is illegal, and the full tank is the base's job to fix.

questions.q: The electric heads flush weakly and the bowl empties slowly. The technician says they are all like that. What do you do?

figure.title: Electric heads, aft cabin
lines: Flush: a trickle, bowl empties in 30 s

options: Accept it; a slow flush is normal for a macerator
Sign; you will clear it yourself with vinegar
Write it on the check-in form and ask for it to be checked before you leave
Sign, and use the forward heads all week
questions.why: A weak flush is a blocked or tired pump that will fail mid-week; note every fault on the form and ask for the fix at the base.

questions.q: The technician hands you this list and says the seacocks are 'all fine'. What do you ask for?
options: To have the list signed by him as checked
To have the bungs counted in the tool bag
To be shown the engine one; the others are small
To be shown each one, turn it yourself, and have a bung tied beside each
questions.why: You need to know where every seacock is and that it turns; a bung tied to the fitting is found in the dark, one in a bag is not.

questions.q: You lift the sole boards and find this. The technician says it is the fridge drain. What do you do?
options: Have it dried out and the fridge drain shown to you, then check it stays dry
Sponge it out yourself and sign; fresh water is harmless
Sign; the automatic pump will take it when it rises
Note 'fridge drain' on the form and sign
questions.why: A dry bilge at check-in is your baseline: any water later is news; a fridge that drains to the bilge is a known source, but it is checked first.

questions.q: The technician says the bilge pumping is 'automatic, you never need it'. How do you check the bilge pumps?

figure.title: Bilge pumps
lines: Electric: float switch under the sole

options: Ask for the pumps' last service date to be written on the form
Lift the float until the pump runs, then find the handle and work the manual pump
Switch the electric pump to 'manual' on the panel and listen for it
Pour a bucket into the bilge and wait for the float to start it
questions.why: The float switch is tested by lifting it, the manual pump by pumping it — and its handle must be where you can find it with water over the sole.

questions.q: The technician opens the gas locker and shows you this. What do you ask for before you sign?

figure.title: Gas locker, cockpit
lines: Locker drain: blocked, 2 cm of water

options: A full spare bottle; the drain can wait for the base
The drain cleared; you will buy a bottle in town
A full spare bottle and the locker drain cleared
A note on the form that the locker holds water
questions.why: Gas is heavier than air: the locker must drain overboard, not into the boat; and a half bottle with no spare runs out mid-week.

questions.q: Tuesday evening at anchor: there is a smell of gas in the galley. What do you do first?

figure.title: Galley, 19:30
lines: Smell of gas by the stove
Stove: off, gas valve at the bottle: open

options: Light a burner to burn off the gas left in the pipe and hose
Pump the bilge and open the gas valve fully to flush the line
Switch on the fan and the lights to look for the leak at the stove
Shut the valve at the bottle, ventilate, no flames or switches until the smell is gone
questions.why: Gas sinks into the bilge: isolate at the bottle, ventilate, no sparks; then find the leak with soapy water on the joints.

questions.q: In the galley you find this. The technician says the alarm 'kept going off, so we disconnected it'. What do you do?

figure.title: Gas alarm
lines: Sensor: in the bilge under the stove
Solenoid switch at the stove: works

options: Ask for it reconnected and tested before departure
Sign and plug it in yourself later
Note it and rely on your nose for the week
Accept it; the solenoid switch is your safety
questions.why: A gas alarm that trips may be finding a real leak; it goes back on and is tested, and the leak is looked for, before you sign.

questions.q: First evening in the marina, your crew start cooking. The stove swings on its gimbals as soon as a pan goes on. What do you tell them?
options: Wedge the stove with a cloth; the lock is for the oven
Lock the gimbals in harbour; free them only at sea so the pan stays level
Lock the gimbals at sea; free them in harbour
Free the gimbals at all times; that is what they are for
questions.why: Gimbals keep the pan level when the boat heels; in a flat harbour the lock stops the stove tipping when someone leans on it.

questions.q: After a night of rain the cockpit looks like this. What do you ask for before you leave the base?

figure.title: Cockpit, Sunday 08:00
lines: Anchor locker: half full of water

options: A bucket; you will bail the cockpit after rain
The scuppers checked; cockpit water drains over the sole
The cockpit drains and the anchor-locker drain cleared and shown to run free
The anchor locker pumped out and the lid taped shut
questions.why: A cockpit that does not drain fills in a sea; a blocked anchor-locker drain puts the water in the forepeak. Both are cleared at the base.

questions.q: You take over the catamaran with this. How do you plan the week's water?
options: Shower ashore only and never touch the watermaker all week
Rely on the watermaker; run it every morning while in the marina
Fill once at the base; 600 l is plenty for 8 people for a week
Fill at every marina and make water only at sea, in clean water; 600 l will not last the week
questions.why: 600 l is under 11 l a day each for 8 people; a watermaker sucks oil and sewage in a harbour — it runs offshore in clean water.

questions.q: The technician switches on the chartplotter, waits for the fix, shows you this and turns to the VHF. What do you ask before he moves on?
options: Whether the card covers the whole cruising ground, and how old the chart is
Whether the plotter also drives the autopilot
Whether the screen can be dimmed for night passages
Nothing — a plotter with a fix is a working plotter
questions.why: Check the chart covers everywhere you will go and ask its edition: an old card misses new marinas, moles and shoals.

questions.q: At the berth the instruments show this, and the base's harbour plan gives 3.0 m here. What has happened?

lines: Harbour plan: 3.0 m at the berth

options: The offset is set below the keel — add the draught
The sounder is set to feet — 9.8 ft is 3.0 m; switch the units to metres
It shows the depth at the harbour mouth, not the berth
The transducer is fouled — the reading is random
questions.why: 9.8 ft = 3.0 m. Greek and Croatian charts are in metres: set depth to metres and distance to nautical miles before you sail.

questions.q: You check the sounder against the harbour plan at the berth. How much water is under the keel right now?

lines: Harbour plan: 3.5 m at the berth

options: 1.4 m — take the draught off the reading
3.3 m — the reading is already the water below the keel
About 1.6 m — the sounder reads from the transducer, not from the keel
3.5 m — the plan is right and the sounder is 0.2 m out
questions.why: No offset: the reading is depth below the transducer, 0.2 m under the surface here. Below the keel: 3.5 − 1.9 ≈ 1.6 m.

questions.q: Going through the plotter, the technician points at the MOB key and moves on. What do you do with it?
options: Press and hold it now to test the DSC distress alert
Note that it is the red button on the VHF handset
Leave it — a casualty is recovered by eye, not from a screen
Ask him to show how it marks and how it clears, then brief the crew on it
questions.why: MOB on the plotter drops a waypoint and shows bearing and distance back; the crew must know where it is before it is needed.

questions.q: On the test run outside the harbour the display shows this. What do you write on the check-in form?
options: Log reads zero — paddle wheel fouled; ask the base to clear it
Nothing — SOG from the plotter does for the week
GPS fault — SOG shows a speed with no log input
Plotter has lost its fix — reboot it at the berth
questions.why: A fouled paddle wheel reads 0; the base pulls and cleans it in the harbour. Note it: speed through the water feeds true wind and the log book.

questions.q: A steady breeze blows across the marina and the burgee flies at the masthead, yet the instruments show this. What do you do?
options: Accept it — the wind shows only once the boat is sailing
Note it — masthead unit dead; ask the base to look at it before you leave
Go up in the bosun's chair and check the sensor yourself
Tap the display — it needs some minutes to warm up
questions.why: The wind instrument should show direction and speed at the berth; a dead one is logged and fixed by the base, not by you aloft.

questions.q: This is the whole of the technician's autopilot briefing. What do you do?

figure.title: Autopilot
lines: Not tried on the test run

options: Accept it — AUTO is the only button you will need
Read the manual the first time you need it at sea
Ask to see Standby, a course change and the alarms, and try it on the test run
Leave it switched off and hand-steer for the week
questions.why: Know how to engage, disengage and what the alarm means before you rely on it — and never in harbours or close quarters.

questions.q: The technician finishes his radio check and leaves the set like this. What do you set before leaving the berth?
options: Channel 16 with squelch fully up to keep it quiet
Leave 72 — the base calls you on it all week
Channel 16 alone — dual watch drains the battery
Channel 16, dual watch on the base's working channel, squelch just above the hiss
questions.why: Under way you keep a watch on 16; dual watch adds the working channel. Squelch fully up mutes weak calls.

questions.q: The technician asks you to do the radio check yourself. How do you make the call?
options: Call the base on its working channel with the boat's name and ask for a readability report
Call the coastguard on channel 16 and ask for a check
Send a DSC test call to the base on channel 70
Call the base on channel 16 — a check must be heard by all
questions.why: Radio checks go on a working channel, not on 16, which is kept for distress, safety and calling.

questions.q: You open the DSC page of the fixed VHF and look at the front of the set. What do you do?
options: Ignore it — DSC is for ships, not charter yachts
Ask for the boat's MMSI to be programmed and the cover replaced before you sign
Program the base's phone number in as the MMSI
Enter the MMSI printed on your own SRC certificate
questions.why: Without the ship's MMSI a DSC alert carries no identity; the cover prevents false alerts. Both are the base's job.

questions.q: The inventory lists a handheld VHF. This is what you find in the chart-table drawer. What do you do?
options: Take it as it is — one bar lasts a week on standby
Have it struck off the inventory to avoid a deposit claim
Ask for the charger and a full charge before you sign, and note it on the form
Leave it — the fixed set is the one that matters
questions.why: The handheld is the radio for the dinghy and the liferaft; flat and without a charger it is useless. Have it charged and listed.

questions.q: The plotter's AIS page shows the harbour traffic. What do you ask the technician?
options: Whether the targets also appear on the VHF screen
Whether it shows yachts as well as ships
Whether the CPA alarm can be switched off at night
Whether it is receive-only or a transponder — can the ferries see you?
questions.why: A receiver shows others to you; only a transponder shows you to them. Know which before you cross a ferry route at night.

questions.q: On the test run, in flat water with no current, you compare the steering compass with the plotter's course over the ground. What do you do?
options: Look for a phone or speaker by the binnacle, then note the deviation that remains
Swing the compass yourself before leaving the harbour
Set the plotter to magnetic north so that the two agree
Accept 8° — that is the variation in the Ionian
questions.why: Compass 090° + 3°E variation = 093° true; the other 5° is deviation — often a phone on the binnacle. Note it; the plotter steers by GPS.
